Cuatro Sillas para Agosto
El fantasma en la habitación nueve no quiere vivir de nuevo. Quiere terminar una canción.
A practical caretaker, a dead singer, and one small show in a lakeside inn. It won't bring him back. It might be enough.

Henry took the caretaker job at the Linden House Inn to fix pipes, not to share room nine with August, a singer who died eleven years ago before his first real show. August's song stops at the third line every time, and he has one week to finish it. Nothing Henry does can buy August back to life. What the reader decides is how to spend a short, whole time with him, and how to say goodbye.
The inn's night clerk, who has heard the parlor piano at 3 AM for years and never told anyone.
If nobody listens, August's song stays stuck on the third line and the waiting stays a waste.

Room Nine
Settle whether August stays, and name what he left unfinished
Room nine, Linden House Inn
Tuesday, 7:40 AM
Henry left his repair ladder by the radiator last night. This morning it stands under the window, perfectly centered, like someone wanted a better seat.
I check the lock. Still bolted from the inside. I check my coffee. Still not strong enough for this.
If you're haunting me, pay rent.
The curtain lifts, though the window is shut. A man is sitting on the top step of the ladder in a wool coat eleven years out of style.
I have an excellent view.
That's not a currency.
It's the only one I've got. I'm August. I was supposed to sing downstairs, once. I never got to the end.
The pipes in this building are older than me and louder than him. I can live with one more thing that knocks at night.
What does Henry do with his new tenant?
Give him the room for one week.
One week. Room nine is yours. In exchange, you tell me what “the end” means.
I stand up on the ladder, which ladders do not enjoy. Nobody has given me a deadline in eleven years. It feels almost like being alive.
Henry writes AUGUST, 7 DAYS on the room board in dry-erase marker. The marker squeaks. The ghost laughs.
Henry gave August room nine for one week in exchange for the truth about his unfinished song.
Ask what's unfinished before promising anything.
Before I sign anything with a dead guy: what's the job?
A song. Four minutes. I get to the third line and it stops, like a record with a scratch in it.
I write SONG on my repair list, between RADIATOR and GUTTERS. It looks less insane in pencil.
Henry asked first; August named his unfinished song, and Henry added it to his repair list without promising a timeline.
Tell him the room is for paying guests.
I open in October. Nine rooms. I can't comp one to a guy who doesn't eat breakfast.
Fair. I'll take the piano bench downstairs. Nobody books a piano bench.
The ladder is back by the radiator. At midnight, the bench in the parlor creaks once, politely, like a guest who knows the rules.
Henry kept room nine for paying guests; August moved to the parlor piano bench on his own terms.
The Third Line
Try to finish the song instead of proving it's perfect
The parlor piano
Thursday, 11:15 PM
The parlor piano is out of tune in a way that sounds almost deliberate. August plays without hands. The keys go down on their own, softly.
He sings two lines in a voice like someone humming into a coat collar. On the third line, he stops. Every time. Same place.
It's a bad song.
Then finish it badly.
You have no artistic fear.
I have plumbing fear. The second-floor bathroom makes a noise like a cow giving birth. That's fear.
I look at the keys instead of him. Eleven years, and I can't get past one line about a porch light.
He isn't stuck on the note. He's stuck on what comes after it.
How does Henry handle the third line?
Sit on the bench and hum the wrong note.
I slide onto the bench and hum the next note wrong. Loudly. On purpose.
That's a B-flat. That's a crime.
He sings the third line just to correct him. Then the fourth, because he's already there. It's ugly. It's the farthest he's gotten in eleven years.
The roof. Tomorrow, midnight. I want to try something I haven't done since I died.
Henry hummed a wrong note on purpose; August corrected it and got past the third line for the first time. August invited him to the roof at midnight.
Offer to fix the piano first.
Maybe it's not you. Maybe it's the F that sticks.
You're giving me an excuse.
I'm giving you a week. Tuning takes time. So does a third line.
Then meet me on the roof tomorrow at midnight. There's something I can do that doesn't need a piano.
Henry started repairing the piano and gave August time instead of pushing the song; August asked him to the roof.
Leave him alone with it.
I'm not a music guy. I'll be in the basement, losing a fight with the water heater.
He goes. Behind him, the piano plays the first two lines again, alone, and stops.
Henry. Tomorrow night, the roof. I'm not asking you to listen. I'm asking you to see something.
Henry gave August privacy with the song; August asked him to the roof anyway.
What Wind Can Do
Respect the only kind of touch a ghost has
The inn roof, by the chimney
Friday, midnight
The roof is flat enough to stand on and old enough to worry about. Henry tested every tar seam before stepping out. August just appeared.
Can I— I mean. Is it possible to touch you?
I don't answer. I lift my hand the way I used to before a first chord, and the air moves.
A breeze, warm for September, runs across the back of Henry's hand. Only his hand. The flag on the dock below doesn't stir.
That's all I can do.
It's not nothing.
Don't be kind about it. You'll want more, and I won't have it.
I had a father who went fast and a marriage that went slow. I know what not enough feels like. This isn't that.
What does Henry offer him?
Give him space to rehearse, and stay nearby.
I'll be over here with a flashlight and the gutter guards. Sing when you want. I won't watch.
I sing to the lake. He installs a gutter guard very badly. It's the best rehearsal I've ever had.
At 1 AM, the wind comes back across his knuckles. A thank-you, or a goodnight. Maybe both.
Henry worked on the roof while August rehearsed without an audience; August thanked him with the wind.
Ask him where the lines are.
Tell me the rules. What's too close?
Don't walk through me. It feels like missing a stair. And don't reach first. Let me.
I put my hand flat on the chimney brick, palm up, and leave it there.
The wind comes. It stays longer this time.
They agreed August reaches first; Henry left his hand open, and August chose to touch it.
Promise to pay whatever it takes to keep him.
There are people who do this. Mediums, whatever. I'll pay. Whatever it costs, you don't have to go.
Henry. I'm not a lease. Nobody gets to renew me.
I step back to the edge of the roof, where the wind can't reach him. Not a punishment. A line.
Henry closes his hand. The song downstairs is still unfinished, but it's August's to finish, not anyone's to buy.
Henry offered to pay to keep August; August refused and drew a line: his staying or leaving is not for sale.
Four Invitations
Keep the show real: a few people who actually want to listen
The front desk
Sunday, 3:00 PM
Henry sets four plain index cards on the front desk. Each says the same thing: Saturday, 7 PM. Parlor. One song. Bring nothing.
I slide the cards toward the drawer with the good stationery. Twice. He slides them back. Twice.
Only four?
Four people who want to listen.
No applause machine?
We can clap badly ourselves.
The last time my name was on a card with a date, I canceled it myself. Nobody knows that. Not even the card.
I am frightened.
Then we start with one verse.
What does Henry do with the four cards?
Let him choose the four guests himself.
I choose. Mrs. Okonjo, who sold me bread when I was nineteen. Pete the plumber, who hums. The night clerk. And you.
Me? I live here.
That's why you get a card. So it's an invitation, not an accident.
August chose the four guests himself, including Henry, so Henry's seat would be an invitation.
Ask for one verse, just for you, first.
No cards yet. One verse, right now, for an audience of one tired handyman.
August sings one verse to the front-desk bell. His voice shakes on “porch light” and doesn't stop.
Fine. Mail the cards. Before I change my mind.
August sang one verse for Henry alone before the invitations went out.
Tell him the show can wait.
You're scared. Then we don't set a date. The cards can sit in a drawer.
No. I did that once. I put the date in a drawer, and then I ran out of dates.
He tells Henry the truth about the show he canceled. The cards go out Monday anyway, because August says so.
Henry offered to postpone; August confessed he had canceled his original show himself and chose to go ahead.
Four Chairs
Sing the song to the end for four people, mistakes and all
The parlor
Saturday, 6:52 PM
Four folding chairs. One lamp. The piano tuned as far as three evenings of online tutorials allow.
It's four chairs, Henry. It looks like a support group.
Four people came for you.
Mrs. Okonjo brought bread, though the card said bring nothing. Pete brought his wife, so technically that's five, and he's standing.
I waited years for a room.
You have one.
Third line coming. Porch light. Don't stop. If I stop now, I stop forever.
The third line arrives. What does Henry do?
Sit in the fourth chair and watch him.
Henry takes the last chair and doesn't look away. At the third line, August's voice cracks. He goes through it anyway.
I sing the whole thing. I get the bridge wrong. Mrs. Okonjo claps like I'm on television.
Four minutes. It's not nothing. It's the opposite of nothing.
August finished the whole song for four people, bridge wrong, while Henry watched from the fourth chair.
Stand by the piano and hum under him.
I stand by the piano. When his voice falters, I hum the note underneath. Badly.
I'm so offended by his flat note that I sail straight through the third line to fix it.
The song ends. Pete says, “Huh,” which from Pete is a standing ovation.
Henry hummed under the third line; August sang through it and finished the song.
Turn off the lamp and give him the dark.
I switch off the lamp. Only the streetlight through the window now.
Thank you. It's easier when nobody can see me either.
He finishes in the dark. When the lamp comes back on, all four guests are crying and pretending they aren't.
Henry turned off the light, and August finished the song in the dark.
One More Morning
Ask for one morning, not forever
The parlor, after the guests leave
Saturday, 11:40 PM
The guests are gone. The folding chairs are still out. August looks thinner at the edges, like a photo left too long in a window.
I can feel it now. Not a door. A draft. I think I could go.
I stack one chair, then stop. If I stack them all, it's over.
Don't ask him to stay. You know what you do to things you won't let go of. You fix them until they break.
One more morning?
One. Because I want it.
Not because you asked. You should know the difference.
How does Henry spend the last night?
Tell him why one morning matters.
My dad went at 4 AM in a hospital hallway. I was in the parking garage. I never got a morning.
I sit in the chair he didn't stack. I stay until he stops talking. Then I stay longer.
Henry told August about missing his father's last morning; August stayed with him through the night.
Keep it light: plan a breakfast.
Then I'm making pancakes you can't eat. You'll watch and suffer.
Blueberry. I want to smell them. I can still do that, a little.
Henry sets an alarm for 5:30 and a bag of frozen blueberries on the counter to thaw, like a promise.
Henry and August planned a blueberry pancake breakfast August could only smell.
Go to bed; let morning come on its own.
I'm not going to watch the clock with you. I'll see you when I see you.
Henry sleeps. At 5 AM, the radiator in his room clanks twice, in the rhythm of the song's first line.
Henry slept instead of keeping vigil; August woke him at 5 AM with the song's rhythm on the radiator.
The Last Morning
Ask to keep the song, and let him go for real
Room nine, by the window
Sunday, 6:48 AM
Light comes in low over the lake. Henry doesn't close the curtain. He thought about it. He kept his hand off the cord.
May I keep the song?
With my name.
Always.
And keep living.
I can miss you and do that.
Then the room was not a waste.
Somewhere there's an ad that says you can talk to your loved ones again. I'll never click it. He was here. That's the whole receipt.
What does Henry say before the light gets high?
Tell him you love him, with no conditions.
I think I'm in love with you. That's not a request. It's just true, and you should hear it once.
I heard it. I'm keeping it. That's allowed, isn't it? Taking something with me?
I put the wind against his cheek. It's the most I have. It's everything I have.
Henry told August he loved him without asking him to stay; August said he'd take it with him and touched his face with the wind.
Tell him he doesn't have to go today.
The draft will still be there next week. You don't owe anyone your leaving. Not even the song.
You mean it? No clock?
A clock. Just not today's.
Henry told August he could leave when he was ready, on a real deadline but not today's.
Thank him, as a friend.
I don't think what I feel is romance. I think you're the best roommate I ever had, and you never paid rent.
I paid in view.
It was a good view.
Henry thanked August as a friend and said plainly that what he felt wasn't romance.
The Porch Light
Choose the goodbye, or a little more time with an end date
The front porch
Sunday, 7:20 AM
The porch light is still on from last night. It's in the song. Henry reaches for the switch and doesn't flip it yet.
Leave it. I wrote that line about a light somebody forgot to turn off for me.
I didn't forget.
I stand on the porch step. The sun comes through me like I'm a screen door.
Whatever happens next, this happened. Nobody can refund it. Nobody can sell it back to me either.
Out on the lake, the fog is lifting. There's one choice left, and it isn't anyone's to buy.
How do they say goodbye?
Say everything, and let him go in the light.
I loved you on day three. You were fighting the water heater, and losing.
Go. I've got your song, with your name on it. I've got an inn to run.
One more morning. I got it. Because I wanted it.
The wind touches Henry's hand once, and then the porch is just a porch. He leaves the light on anyway.
August confessed and left in the morning light; Henry kept the song with August's name on it and went on living.
Ask him to stay until first snow, and write.
Not forever. Until the first snow. Write something with me that isn't about dying.
A song about plumbing.
A song about plumbing.
The room board says AUGUST, CO-WRITER. The end date is written in pen, not dry-erase. They both agreed to that.
August chose to stay until the first snow as Henry's co-writer, with the end date agreed and written in pen.
Say goodbye as friends, on the porch.
You were a friend when I needed one. Go easy.
You threw me the best show of my life, and I'm dead. That's a real review.
Four chairs, Henry. It was enough.
August goes the way fog goes, with no moment you can point to. The fourth chair stays out in the parlor all winter.
Henry and August said goodbye as friends; the fourth chair stayed out all winter.
One More Morning

The song is finished and the confession is said. August leaves in the morning light because he's ready, not because anyone paid or pleaded. Henry keeps the song with August's name on it and keeps living. It isn't forever, and it was never meant to be.
One more morning. I got it. Because I wanted it.
Until the First Snow
August isn't ready to go, and Henry doesn't make him. They agree on a season, not a lifetime, and write songs together until the first snow. The end date is in pen. They both chose it.
Until the first snow. Then you open the window.
Four Chairs Was Enough
Henry doesn't want romance, and he says so. He still gives August the show and a good goodbye, and they part as friends. The fourth chair stays out all winter.
Four chairs, Henry. It was enough.
